Careers Internships & Fellowships Apprenticeships & Workforce Development Work at DOE Funding Opportunities Breadcrumb Biological and Environmental Research Redesigned Hepatitis C Drug Becomes a Powerful New Treatment for COVID-19 Redesigned Hepatitis C Drug Becomes a Powerful New Treatment for COVID-19 Scientists transformed an old drug into a potent COVID-19 treatment effective against drug-resistant variants. Biological and Environmental Research February 19, 2026 Estimated Read Time 3 min The final version of the redesigned drug binds tightly to the main COVID-19 protease, an enzyme the virus needs to multiply. The drug’s structure is effective even against mutated forms that resist other treatments. Image courtesy of Stanford University The Science Researchers have redesigned the hepatitis C drug boceprevir to create a more effective treatment for COVID-19. Some virus variants no longer respond well to current therapies, like Paxlovid, due to mutations in the main COVID-19 virus protease (Mpro). This is a key enzyme the virus uses to replicate. Mpro is essential to the virus and remains intact from variant to variant. As such, it is an ideal target for treatments to focus on. Using X-ray crystal structures, scientists refined boceprevir atom by atom. They worked to improve how the drug binds within key pockets of the enzyme. The researchers used the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (a DOE Office of Science User Facility) to analyze the crystal structure when the drug was attached to Mpro. The Impact This research produced a drug that is effective against COVID-19 strains that are resistant to existing treatments. The resulting compound, ML2006a4, binds more tightly and durably than earlier drugs. It also shows superior protection in preclinical animal studies. By redesigning an older hepatitis C drug, scientists made it more effective against mutated forms of the virus’s protease. This could help doctors treat patients who no longer respond to existing therapies. Summary Boceprevir is a protease inhibitor originally developed to treat hepatitis C. Scientists adapted this drug to target the main protease (Mpro) of SARS-CoV-2. This is a critical enzyme the virus uses to process its polyproteins and replicate. Because Mpro is conserved across variants and has no close human equivalent, it remains a prime target for antiviral drug development. However, some SARS-CoV-2 variants contain mutations in Mpro that reduce the effectiveness of existing treatments. Using X-ray crystallography data collected at the Macromolecular Crystallography Beamlines at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL), researchers determined high-resolution structures of Mpro bound to various boceprevir analogs. These structural insights guided a stepwise redesign of the molecule to improve its fit within the enzyme’s active site and sub-pockets. The team optimized interactions and reduced internal strains within the drug’s structure to improve binding, potency, and resistance profile. The final compound, ML2006a4, binds covalently to Mpro and retains strong activity even against variants harboring resistance-associated mutations. This structure-guided approach demonstrates how iterative design can yield next-generation antivirals with broad-spectrum activity. It also underscores the vital role of DOE- and NIH-supported synchrotron-based methods in accelerating drug discovery against emerging viral threats. Contact Michael Lin Stanford University mzlin@stanford.edu Funding Funding for this research included: Sarafan ChEM-H and the Innovative Medicines Accelerator, Harrington Scholar-Innovator Award, Emergent Ventures at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University, Stanford-Coulter Translational Research Grant, National Institute of Health(NIH)/National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Antiviral Drug Discovery (AViDD) Center, the Denver Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Stanford Bio-X Program and a Bio-X Interdisciplinary Graduate Student Fellowship, E&M Foundation Postdoctoral Fellowship, Postdoctoral Fellowship in Translational Medicine from the PhRMA Foundation and an anonymous donation to establish the Stanford BSL3 facility. The research used resources at SSRL, a DOE Office of Science user facility, and of the SSRL Structural Molecular Biology Program supported by the DOE Office of Biological and Environmental Research and by NIH National Institute of General Medical Sciences. Publications Westberg, M., et al. “An orally bioavailable SARS-CoV-2 main protease inhibitor exhibits improved affinity and reduced sensitivity to mutations”, Sci. Transl. Med. 16, eadi0979 (2024). [DOI: 10.1126/scitranslmed.adi0979] Related Links Going atom-by-atom, Stanford researchers craft a new precision drug for fighting COVID-19, Stanford Report

epidemiological situation via the WHO COVID-19 dashboard. If data for certain countries is unavailable in this section, it may indicate that they have either ceased reporting COVID-19 surveillance data to WHO or have integrated the COVID-19 surveillance into existing respiratory disease surveillance. In the latter case, SARS-CoV-2 detections from sentinel and systematic virological surveillance sites in those countries may be found in the Circulation section which also includes information on SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation. This global summary of COVID-19 cases includes data on confirmed cases reported to WHO from the comprehensive COVID-19 case monitoring. Coronavirus (COVID-19) cases, %%COUNTRY%% data Source: World Health Organization Loading... Loading... Loading... What is the definition of 'confirmed' and 'reported' in COVID-19 data? All data represents the date of reporting as opposed to date of symptom onset. All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. In the context of WHO's statistical reporting of COVID-19 data, it is important to note that only confirmed cases are included in case and death counts. In guidance updated on 22 July 2023; there are two alternative definitions for 'Confirmed case of SARS-CoV-2 infection' in international surveillance reporting, although some departures may exist due to local adaptations: a) A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT), regardless of clinical criteria OR epidemiological criteria. b) A person meeting clinical criteria AND/OR epidemiological criteria (suspect case A) with a positive professional-use or self-test SARS-CoV-2 Antigen-RDT. Additionally, WHO only disseminates data as reported by its Member States. From the 31 December 2019 to the 21 March 2020, WHO collected the numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths through official communications under the International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), complemented by monitoring the official ministries of health websites and social media accounts. Since 22 March 2020, global data has been compiled through WHO region-specific dashboards, and/or aggregate count data reported directly to WHO headquarters by Member States. Statistical counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Case detection, definitions, testing strategies, reporting practice, and lag times (e.g. time to case notification, and time to reporting of deaths) differ between countries, territories and areas. These factors, amongst others, influence the counts presented with variable under or overestimation of true case and death counts, and variable delays to reflecting these statistics at a global level. Please note that statistics do not necessarily reflect the actual number of cases and deaths or the actual number of countries where cases and deaths are occurring, as a number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting. Trends in COVID-19 cases, %%COUNTRY%% Recent COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, July 2023 - present Source: World Health Organization Data may be incomplete for the latest week. Total COVID-19 cases reported to WHO (weekly) %%COUNTRY%%, January 2020 - present Source: World Health Organization Why is COVID-19 data being presented as weekly statistics? A number of countries have stopped reporting or changed their frequency of reporting COVID-19 case and death counts to WHO. An outcome of these differences in reporting is that WHO may receive daily data from some countries, while other countries may only report data to WHO once every 14 days. In addition, countries differ in how they choose to report statistics; some countries provide their data attributed to specific dates while others who report less frequently may group data from 7 days into a single statistic attributed to a week in their reporting. As of 25 August 2023, WHO declared that it is no longer necessary for Member States to report daily counts of cases and deaths to WHO and requested strengthening of weekly reporting. Reported data is still available attributed to specific dates (daily data) here as a download. This dashboard presents the same statistics as weekly figures in charts in order to mitigate against the visual misinterpretation of data. Should daily data have been presented here, many countries would show zero counts for multiple consecutive days due in part to the differences in how they choose to report. While weekly intervals do not completely mitigate against this, the approach reduces the risk that some dashboard users might infer zero cases or deaths when lack of data is often due to reporting differences. What do negative counts of cases or deaths mean? All data is subject to continuous verification and may change based on retrospective updates to accurately reflect trends, changes in country case definitions and/or reporting practices. Significant data errors detected or reported to WHO may be corrected by Member States at more frequent intervals with some countries performing retrospective bulk corrections in their reporting. Bulk corrections may lead to the appearance of significant spikes or negative values which are verified and validated by WHO. Last 28 days ‘Last 28 days’ refers to the four preceding most recently complete epidemiological weeks. WHO Regions The World Health Organization (WHO) is divided into six regions with regional offices, each responsible for addressing health challenges and promoting public health within its designated geographical area. These regions serve as administrative units that allow the WHO to tailor its efforts to the specific needs, priorities, and health conditions of member countries within each region. World Bank Income Groups The World Bank classifies economies into income groups based on their Gross National Income (GNI) per capita. These annually updated classifications help the World Bank and other organizations analyze and understand global economic trends, allocate resources, and design development policies. WHO COVID-19 Dashboard is updated every Tuesday for the period of two full weeks prior. Counts include both domestic and repatriated cases. Apply Departments Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Biostatistics Environmental Health and Engineering Epidemiology Health Policy and Management Health, Behavior and Society International Health Mental Health Molecular Microbiology and Immunology Population, Family and Reproductive Health Faculty Topics Bloomberg School What to Know About Flu, COVID-19, and RSV This Fall Influenza activity is increasing, while RSV and COVID case numbers remain low. Published November 04, 2026 By Morgan Coulson COVID-19 Infectious Diseases Medicine Vaccines As we head into the late fall and winter months, flu cases are beginning to rise in parts of the U.S., even as overall respiratory virus activity remains low. The CDC is predicting a relatively moderate respiratory virus season, similar to last year’s, when weekly hospitalizations from flu, COVID-19, and RSV peaked at around 16 per 100,000 people. But that’s no reason to put off vaccination, explains Andrew Pekosz, PhD, a professor in Molecular Microbiology and Immunology: “This is a good last call to get your influenza vaccination for this year, because vaccines work best when taken before the influenza season starts.” This season also brings a new option for some adults: a recently approved mRNA influenza vaccine for people ages 50 and older. “The hope is that the new mRNA vaccine will produce a better immune response against influenza and, therefore, provide better protection,” says Anna Durbin, MD, a professor in International Health and director of the Center for Immunization Research. In this Q&A, adapted from an October 29 media briefing, Pekosz and Durbin discuss emerging respiratory virus trends, what we know about this season’s vaccines, and how people can protect themselves and others as the season progresses. What is the current situation with influenza in the United States? Andrew Pekosz: Influenza activity is low but increasing, particularly in the western and southern U.S. This is early, but not unheard of. The cases seem to be driven by a variant of the H1N1 influenza virus, which has some new mutations compared with last year’s H1N1 virus. Those mutations allow it to escape some of the immunity in the population. However, data suggest this year’s influenza vaccine can recognize this variant. Influenza vaccines cover three different viruses, and usually different influenza viruses cause infections at the beginning and end of the flu season. So, even if you hear about a potential mismatch with the H1N1 component, it’s important to get the vaccine because the other two components look like they’re going to be pretty good matches for the viruses emerging early in the flu season. How well do this season’s COVID and RSV vaccines match the strains circulating now? AP: For COVID, we’re seeing low but steady activity. We expect another increase in cases sometime in December or January. We haven’t seen much RSV activity this year, which is somewhat unusual. However, I expect we’ll begin seeing RSV cases in the next couple of weeks. Now is the time to get your COVID and RSV vaccines, if you’re eligible, along with influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, to prepare for the respiratory virus season. Both the COVID and RSV vaccines are very good matches for the viruses currently circulating. The RSV vaccine is recommended for a more limited group of individuals, particularly those ages 75 and older, as well as people with certain underlying conditions or who are immunocompromised. That vaccine has demonstrated very good efficacy over the past few years. [Note: The RSV vaccine is not currently an annual vaccine, per the CDC.] What’s the difference between the new mRNA flu vaccine and the traditional vaccine? Anna Durbin: Essentially, the mRNA vaccine enters your cells and instructs them to make the flu protein against which your body produces antibodies. The cells make that protein and then present it to your immune system, exposing the immune system to the protein, or antigen. Current traditional flu vaccines, by contrast, contain proteins that stimulate an immune response. Unlike mRNA vaccines, they don’t enter the cells in the same way to stimulate the broadest possible immune response. Traditional vaccines generate a good antibody response but may not stimulate other parts of the immune system as effectively as mRNA vaccines do. Which is more effective? AD: We don’t have data from the current flu season yet. However, the clinical trials used to support the mRNA vaccine’s approval showed that, in people ages 50 and older, it performed better than traditional vaccines. One important consideration is that adults ages 65 and older receive a higher dose of the traditional flu vaccines than younger people. The mRNA vaccine was not directly compared in clinical trials with those high-dose vaccines in people ages 65 and older. However, we know that the antibody responses generated by the mRNA flu vaccine in people ages 65 and older were at least as good as those generated by traditional flu vaccines. Until we get good real-world efficacy data from the flu season, we won’t know for sure. How is the mRNA vaccine different from a public health standpoint? AD: The advantage of an mRNA influenza vaccine is that it can be produced very quickly. For instance, if a new strain emerges over the summer, the [fall] vaccine [for that year] could potentially be changed to match it. Right now, the FDA holds a meeting every March to select which strains will be included in the influenza vaccine. That meeting happens so early because it takes a long time to produce traditional influenza vaccines. The hope with an mRNA vaccine is that we might be able to hold another meeting in July or August and update the vaccine if the circulating strains have changed. We’re not there yet. The agency is discussing and exploring that possibility, and I think a lot will depend on the evidence generated by this new mRNA influenza vaccine. How can a person tell whether they have the flu, COVID, a cold, or something else? AP: Usually, you can distinguish a cold from something more significant or serious by the effect it has on your ability to breathe and by the severity of your cough. If you have difficulty breathing, that can mean the infection is spreading deeper into your lungs. In that case, it may not be a common cold but one of the other respiratory viruses. There are some useful at-home testing kits that can help determine whether you're infected with influenza, RSV, or COVID-19. Knowing which virus you have is particularly important if you’re in a high-risk group for severe illness. Antiviral treatments are available for influenza and COVID-19, and they have been shown to reduce the duration of symptoms and the likelihood of developing severe illness. The key is that you need to start these antivirals soon after symptoms begin. Be proactive. Keep some at-home tests available, and if you test positive for one of these viruses, contact your pharmacy to make sure you can get the appropriate antiviral medication and begin taking it as soon as possible. What should immunocompromised people and adults ages 65 and older do this fall? AD: Immunocompromised people and adults older than 65 should get vaccinated. We also know from many studies that adults over 65 often get infected by their grandchildren and other children. Get young children vaccinated against influenza, not only for older adults’ protection but also because influenza can cause serious complications in children, including death. How long after vaccination does it take for protection to develop? AP: It takes about two weeks for influenza vaccine protection to reach its maximum level. That protection then lasts for several weeks to several months after vaccination. Getting vaccinated before influenza becomes widespread will provide the greatest protection against disease. What is the most important thing for primary care physicians to know about this flu season? AD: Influenza can be a very serious illness. The CDC reported almost 5,000 laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalizations nationwide during the week ending October 17. This is the highest early-season hospitalization rate for mid-October since the 2010–2011 flu season. [The following week, ending October 24, that number rose to 6,100 hospitalizations nationwide, according to the CDC.] I think it’s really important, particularly for older adults who are at greater risk of severe influenza, to get vaccinated. What I tell my patients, and what I encourage other physicians to tell their patients, is that a flu vaccine is the best way to protect yourself against influenza, and to get vaccinated as soon as possible. Fewer people are getting the flu vaccine, or they are getting it later in the season. What is the impact of this? AD: We do think that, overall, fewer people are getting vaccinated against various diseases, which increases the risk of infection. Unfortunately, when fewer people get vaccinated, influenza can spread more easily, resulting in more infections and potentially serious consequences for people’s health. There are a lot of questions people have about vaccines, and there’s been a lot of misinformation circulating. I encourage people to talk with their physicians. Researchers sequenced 535 SARS-CoV-2 whole genomes from clinical samples collected in Duhok, a city in northern Iraq, between June 2021 and February 2022, a window that captured both the Delta and Omicron waves. By reconstructing the viruses’ spatiotemporal spread with discrete Bayesian phylogeographic modeling, the team traced when each variant arrived, where it came from, and whether border controls changed the course of the epidemics. The analysis showed that the Delta variant entered Iraq roughly three months before the government enacted its travel ban on India, the country then associated with the variant’s explosive growth. Genetic evidence indicated that most Delta introductions originated from Western and Southern Asia rather than from a single recognizable epicenter. By the time the ban was announced, the variant had already seeded community transmission inside the country, so the restriction could not have prevented the wave that followed. Omicron told a similar story from a different starting point. That variant slipped into Iraq even though the tourist travel restriction was already in force, demonstrating that an active border policy did not stop the newest variant of concern from arriving and spreading. The researchers concluded that both variants had established sustained community transmission despite the restrictions in place, rendering the measures ineffective for the purposes they were intended to serve. The study’s context matters for interpreting these results. Iraq and its neighbors in Western Asia sequenced less than one percent of SARS-CoV-2 cases in 2021, leaving the region with sparse genomic surveillance. The authors note that the effectiveness of travel restrictions in mitigating the spread of novel viral variants remains understudied, particularly in such settings. Their work aimed to determine whether the restrictions delayed variant introduction, postponed the onset of community transmission, or altered the geographic sources of viral introductions over time. On all three counts, the restrictions fell short. Phylogeographic modeling, the core method of the study, uses the mutations accumulated in viral genomes to infer where lineages traveled and when. Discrete Bayesian approaches treat each sampled location as a state and estimate the probability of transitions between states across the phylogenetic tree, yielding dated estimates of introduction events and their origins. Applied to the Duhok sequences, this framework allowed the team to distinguish viruses that had been circulating locally for months from those that had arrived recently, and to attribute introductions to broad source regions. The findings extend beyond Iraq. When the researchers examined travel restrictions on a global scale, they report similar patterns of limited efficacy in mitigating the introductions of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants. The underlying reason, they argue, is structural: variants of concern typically spread internationally before they are detected anywhere, so border controls enacted after a variant is recognized arrive too late to contain it. Cryptic spread, the movement of the virus through undetected infections and under-sampled regions, undermines policies that target only the countries where a variant has been publicly identified. The authors also raise a second-order concern. Border controls, they suggest, may discourage countries from transparent reporting, because governments that identify a new variant first can face immediate travel bans from other states. That dynamic creates a perverse incentive to delay announcing discoveries, which would further slow the global detection of emerging variants and deepen the surveillance gaps that already hamper response efforts in low-sequencing regions. As an alternative, the study points to rapid genomic sequencing paired with real-time international data sharing as the most effective tools against emerging variants of concern. Sequencing detects a variant’s presence within a country’s borders regardless of where it came from, and open data sharing lets other nations adjust their own surveillance before the variant reaches them. The authors argue that public health responses should prioritize vaccination alongside proven non-pharmaceutical measures, which they enumerate as stay-at-home orders, mask mandates, restrictions on gatherings to fewer than ten people, and the closure of high-exposure businesses, schools, and universities. The study carries some caveats inherent to its design. The sequencing was concentrated in a single city, Duhok, so the picture of national spread depends on phylogeographic inference rather than uniform sampling across Iraq. The work was also conducted in a region with minimal surveillance capacity, which is precisely the condition the authors identify as enabling cryptic spread. The article was released as a shared early version, citable with a permanent DOI and subject to further edits before the final version of record appears. Even so, the central result is difficult to reconcile with targeted border closures: by the time a variant is named, it has often already arrived. That variant slipped into Iraq even though the tourist travel restriction was already in force, demonstrating that an active border policy did not stop the newest variant of concern from arriving and spreading. The researchers concluded that both variants had established sustained community transmission despite the restrictions in place, rendering the measures ineffective for the purposes they were intended to serve. Discover more Get Rapid Tests Find Lung Care Read Med Journals Study Biology Check Symptoms The study’s context matters for interpreting these results. Iraq and its neighbors in Western Asia sequenced less than one percent of SARS-CoV-2 cases in 2021, leaving the region with sparse genomic surveillance. The authors note that the effectiveness of travel restrictions in mitigating the spread of novel viral variants remains understudied, particularly in such settings. Their work aimed to determine whether the restrictions delayed variant introduction, postponed the onset of community transmission, or altered the geographic sources of viral introductions over time. On all three counts, the restrictions fell short. Phylogeographic modeling, the core method of the study, uses the mutations accumulated in viral genomes to infer where lineages traveled and when. Discrete Bayesian approaches treat each sampled location as a state and estimate the probability of transitions between states across the phylogenetic tree, yielding dated estimates of introduction events and their origins. Applied to the Duhok sequences, this framework allowed the team to distinguish viruses that had been circulating locally for months from those that had arrived recently, and to attribute introductions to broad source regions. The findings extend beyond Iraq. When the researchers examined travel restrictions on a global scale, they report similar patterns of limited efficacy in mitigating the introductions of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants. The underlying reason, they argue, is structural: variants of concern typically spread internationally before they are detected anywhere, so border controls enacted after a variant is recognized arrive too late to contain it. Cryptic spread, the movement of the virus through undetected infections and under-sampled regions, undermines policies that target only the countries where a variant has been publicly identified. The authors also raise a second-order concern. Border controls, they suggest, may discourage countries from transparent reporting, because governments that identify a new variant first can face immediate travel bans from other states. That dynamic creates a perverse incentive to delay announcing discoveries, which would further slow the global detection of emerging variants and deepen the surveillance gaps that already hamper response efforts in low-sequencing regions. Discover more Browse Reference travel ban travel bans Plan Vacations Apply for Visas As an alternative, the study points to rapid genomic sequencing paired with real-time international data sharing as the most effective tools against emerging variants of concern. Sequencing detects a variant’s presence within a country’s borders regardless of where it came from, and open data sharing lets other nations adjust their own surveillance before the variant reaches them. The authors argue that public health responses should prioritize vaccination alongside proven non-pharmaceutical measures, which they enumerate as stay-at-home orders, mask mandates, restrictions on gatherings to fewer than ten people, and the closure of high-exposure businesses, schools, and universities. The study carries some caveats inherent to its design. The sequencing was concentrated in a single city, Duhok, so the picture of national spread depends on phylogeographic inference rather than uniform sampling across Iraq. The work was also conducted in a region with minimal surveillance capacity, which is precisely the condition the authors identify as enabling cryptic spread. The article was released as a shared early version, citable with a permanent DOI and subject to further edits before the final version of record appears. Even so, the central result is difficult to reconcile with targeted border closures: by the time a variant is named, it has often already arrived. Than Flu Shots Author(s)Sabrina McCrear Fact checked by: Maggie L. Shaw SIRVA was rare after COVID-19 and flu shots, but COVID-19 vaccination had about 7 more cases per 100,000 doses in a study of 1.8 million. Advertisement Although rare, the absolute risk of shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA) after COVID-19 or flu vaccination should be considered alongside the established benefits of both vaccines, according to a recent study published in JAMA Internal Medicine.1 Adverse events or injection site reactions are not uncommon from vaccines. SIRVA was added to the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program vaccine injury table in 2017 based on accumulating case series. Epidemiological studies of SIRVA have been limited because the condition lacks specific diagnostic codes, is rare, must be distinguished from transient postvaccination reactions, and its long-term prognosis remains poorly characterized. Prior case reports and surveillance studies have noted instances of SIRVA after COVID-19 vaccination; however, they could not quantify its incidence relative to other routinely administered vaccines. In 2024, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine identified this as an important evidence gap.1 Comparing SIRVA Risk Across More Than 1.8 Million Vaccinations The retrospective cohort study was conducted at Kaiser Permanente Southern California (KPSC), an integrated health care system whose prepaid model captures member data, including sociodemographics, encounters, diagnoses, laboratory tests, pharmacy use, and vaccinations. KPSC members 18 years or older who received a COVID-19 or flu vaccine between August 1, 2023, and April 30, 2024, were included in the analysis. A SIRVA case was defined by 5 required criteria: anatomical concordance with the vaccination arm, symptom onset within 7 days of vaccination, symptom duration greater than 30 days to exclude transient reactogenicity events, vaccination identified as a possible cause, and no other identifiable causes for the shoulder condition. There were 1,366,362 individuals who met the criteria for the study across 1,901,588 vaccinations. The mean age was 58.4 years, and 782,994 (57.3%) were female individuals. Among eligible vaccinations, 313,571 (16.5%) were received by Asian or other Pacific Islander individuals; 134,951 (7.1%) by Black individuals; 704,502 (37.0%) by Hispanic individuals; 667,597 (35.1%) by White individuals; and 80,967 (4.3%) by individuals of multiple, other, or unknown race and ethnicity. Of the eligible vaccinations, 70,952 (3.7%) were simultaneous COVID-19 and influenza vaccinations and therefore were excluded from the primary analysis. Overall, the final analysis included 1,830,636 vaccinations, of which 1,234,022 were for the flu and 596,614 were for COVID-19. Of the COVID-19 vaccines, 99.98% were Pfizer-BioNTech mRNA. Of the flu vaccines, 66.40% were standard-dose inactivated quadrivalent influenza vaccine (SD-IIV4), and 33.58% were high-dose inactivated quadrivalent influenza vaccine (HD-IIV4). In a CDC survey of more than 12,500 people who received a third dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna vaccine, 79.4% reported local injection site reactions like itching or redness and 74.1% reported systemic reactions like fatigue, muscle aches, and headaches. Systemic reactions mostly occurred the day after receiving the shot.2 These findings show how common short-term reactions are after COVID-19 vaccination, which the SIRVA case definition excluded by requiring symptoms to last more than 30 days. SIRVA Incidence Higher After COVID-19 Vaccination Researchers identified 252 SIRVA cases: 110 after a COVID-19 vaccination and 142 after a flu vaccination. SIRVA incidence was 1.84 per 10,000 COVID-19 vaccinations compared with 1.15 per 10,000 flu vaccinations (adjusted relative risk [aRR], 1.63; 95% CI, 1.16-2.28), or approximately 7 additional cases per 100,000 vaccinations. SIRVA incidence increased with age after both vaccines. However, among adults 65 years or older, SIRVA risk did not differ significantly between COVID-19 vaccination and HD-IIV4, a recommended influenza vaccine for this age group (aRR, 1.41; 95% CI, 0.92-2.15). COVID-19 vaccination was associated with a significantly higher risk than SD-IIV4 in older adults, but that comparison was based on only 9 SIRVA cases after SD-IIV4. Furthermore, the median time to the first shoulder-related encounter was 46 days after influenza vaccination and 51.5 days after COVID-19 vaccination, even though 94.7% of confirmed cases had symptom onset within 2 days of vaccination. The study had several limitations. Case identification relied on patients seeking care and on clinical documentation, which may underestimate true SIRVA incidence. Its observational design limits causal inference, and residual confounding from unmeasured factors, such as needle length, injection site within the deltoid, or undiagnosed shoulder conditions, may persist. Also, results from a single health system using mostly Pfizer-BioNTech doses during 1 season may not be generalizable. "Despite the higher incidence after COVID-19 vaccination, the benefits of COVID-19 and influenza vaccination in preventing severe disease and hospitalization may outweigh the small absolute and relative risks of SIRVA," the study authors wrote.1 References 1. Back to Healio Save Share LinkedIn Facebook X (Twitter) Bluesky Threads Email Copy Link Key takeaways: Patients with immune-mediated disease hospitalized for COVID-19 had an overall mortality rate of 28% in 2024. The findings highlight the need for research to determine vaccine strategies for this population. ORLANDO — Time since last booster, but not vaccination status or total number of doses, was independently associated with mortality in patients with immune-mediated rheumatic diseases who were hospitalized for COVID-19, said a presenter here. Vitor Cruz, MD, PhD, of the Federal University of Goias, in Brazil, presented data at ACR Convergence demonstrating that mortality, while declining over time, remains substantial among patients with immune-mediated rheumatic diseases who are hospitalized for COVID-19, with a rate of 28% in 2024. “Patients with immune-mediated rheumatic diseases are particularly vulnerable to severe COVID-19, especially those receiving immunosuppressive therapies,” Cruz told Healio regarding his presentation. “Although vaccination has significantly improved protection against severe disease, we still need to better understand how this protection changes over time. “Our study was important because we analyzed real-world data from a nationwide Brazilian surveillance system, focusing on hospitalized patients with immune-mediated rheumatic diseases,” Cruz added. “We wanted to investigate not only vaccination status and the number of vaccine doses received, but also whether the time elapsed since the last booster was associated with in-hospital mortality.” To examine in-hospital COVID-19 mortality trends and factors among patients with immune-mediated rheumatic diseases, Cruz and colleagues conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study of data from the Brazilian Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Surveillance System. The analysis included a total of 918 patients of all ages who had been hospitalized with COVID-19 related severe acute respiratory syndrome between 2022 and 2024. The researchers used multivariable logistic regression models to examine factors associated with all-cause in-hospital mortality. Vaccination status, total number of doses and time elapsed since the last booster dose were evaluated. According to the researchers, overall in-hospital mortality during the study period was 36%. Over the years, the mortality rate declined from 38% in 2022 to 26% in 2023, then climbed to 28% in 2024. Independent predictors of mortality were older age (OR = 1.01 per year; 95% CI, 1-1.02), Black race/ethnicity (OR = 2.22; 95% CI, 1.08-4.57), immunosuppression (OR = 2; 95% CI, 1.41-2.83), cardiopathy (OR = 1.37; 95% CI, 1.02-1.83), dyspnea (OR = 1.84; 95% CI, 1.37-2.47), respiratory distress (OR = 2.08; 95% CI, 1.54-2.71), an oxygen saturation rate of less than 95% (OR = 2.07; 95% CI, 1.54-2.76), ICU admission (OR = 4.89; 95% CI, 3.58-6.68), and ventilatory support (OR = 4.88; 95% CI, 3.31-7.2), the researchers wrote. Notably, longer duration since a patient’s last booster dose was independently associated with an increased risk for mortality (OR = 1.97; 95% CI, 1.09-3.59), even after adjusting for immunosuppression, the researchers wrote. Meanwhile, neither overall vaccination status (OR = 0.86; 95% CI, 0.45-1.63) nor total number of vaccine doses (OR = 1; 95% CI, 0.89-1.12) were associated with mortality. “Our findings reinforce the importance of keeping COVID-19 vaccination up to date in patients with immune-mediated rheumatic diseases, particularly those receiving immunosuppressive treatment,” Cruz told Healio. “From a clinical perspective, physicians should pay attention not only to whether their patients have been vaccinated, but also to when they received their most recent booster. “However, our study was observational and included only hospitalized patients,” he added. “Therefore, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence supporting a specific booster interval or more frequent vaccination schedules. Rather, they highlight the potential importance of timely booster vaccination and the need for further research to define optimal vaccination strategies for this population.” For more information: Vitor Cruz, MD, PhD, can be reached at vitorcruz@ufg.br. records.content: Skip to content Bsky Twitter TikTok YouTube Facebook Instagram Wisconsin Watch Nonprofit, nonpartisan news about Wisconsin Free newsletters Become a supporter Sign In Open Search Search for: Search Become a supporter Menu Sign In About us Open dropdown menu Our people Our Board of Directors Our ethics Our funding Our impact Support our work Open dropdown menu Ways to give or donate Join the Watchdog Club or Leadership Circle Join the Legacy Society Coverage areas Open dropdown menu State government Data Centers Watch Education & Employment Agriculture & Environment Health & Welfare Justice & Safety Community Opinion Major projects Open dropdown menu Forward Northeast News Fact Briefs Data tools Supreme costs Forgotten homes Prison Problems Q&Aging Latest stories Events Posted inHealth & Welfare What you need to know about COVID-19, flu and RSV vaccines Health experts expect another challenging respiratory virus season, but vaccines help provide protection. by Valeria Ricciulli / Public Good News November 6, 2026November 5, 2026 Why you can trust Wisconsin Watch Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Threads (Opens in new window) Threads Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit Add Wisconsin Watch to Google (Prostock-Studio / iStock) Reading Time: 4 minutes What you need to know Immunizations against COVID-19, the flu and RSV are available now. Recommendations vary depending on your age, health and other risk factors. Earlier in the fall is a good time to get vaccinated against respiratory viruses, and you can get multiple vaccines at the same appointment. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention predicts that COVID-19, the flu and RSV could cause a similar number of hospitalizations this fall and winter as they did last season. Last fall and winter, the U.S. experienced its highest levels of respiratory illness in more than 25 years. According to preliminary data from the CDC, millions of people were infected with the flu, at least 390,000 were hospitalized for it, and 24,000 died from it. This year, the agency predicts that COVID-19, the flu and RSV could cause a similar number of cases and hospitalizations. The good news is that immunizations to protect against all three viruses are now available, and most eligible people can get them for free. “Respiratory viruses sicken and even kill thousands of people every year,” Dr. Preeti Malani, infectious disease physician and professor at the University of Michigan, tells Public Good News. “Vaccination is a safe and effective way to help prevent illness and prevent severe illness.” Read on to learn more about the immunizations available, who should get them this season and when. Which immunizations are available this fall and winter, and who are they recommended for? Updated COVID-19 and flu vaccines are available this respiratory virus season, along with RSV immunizations for certain groups. This year, a new mRNA flu vaccine option, Moderna’s mFlusiva, is available for people 50 and older. We talked to experts about the immunization options for each virus and who they’re recommended for, following guidance from major medical associations like the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Family Physicians. COVID-19 Who should get the vaccine? All adults 19 and older, especially those 65 and over and people at higher risk of severe COVID-19, such as people with diabetes, heart disease, chronic lung diseases, or cancer. Children ages 6 to 23 months. Malani explains that young children “have lost immunity provided by their mothers after birth and their own immune system is still immature.” Children and teens ages 2 to 18 years who are at increased risk of severe COVID-19, have never been vaccinated or live with someone at high risk. Vaccination is also an option for other children whose parents want them protected. People who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease specialist and professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, says that these maternal antibodies can help protect newborns. What COVID-19 vaccines are available this season? mRNA vaccines: Made by Pfizer and Moderna, these vaccines give your cells instructions to produce a harmless piece of the virus, which helps your immune system recognize and fight it. Protein-based vaccine: Novavax offers a vaccine that uses a protein from the virus to trigger an immune response. This may appeal to people who prefer a vaccine without mRNA technology. Both types help protect against severe COVID-19, and neither is generally recommended over the other for people who are eligible for both. Flu Who should get the vaccine? Everyone 6 months and older. Vaccination is especially important for young children, older adults, pregnant people, and people with certain underlying health conditions. What flu vaccines are available this season? Standard flu shots: These are appropriate for most people ages 6 months and older. Some are made using eggs, while others are egg-free. People with egg allergies can generally get any flu vaccine, including egg-based vaccines, because they contain only a very small amount of egg protein. However, your doctor may recommend that you wait after your vaccine for observation as an extra precaution. Nasal spray vaccine: FluMist is a needle-free option for eligible people ages 2 to 49 years old. It can also be administered at home in some states, but it isn’t recommended for people who are pregnant or immunocompromised or have certain other medical conditions. Vaccines for older adults: Adults 65 and older are advised to get an enhanced flu vaccine, which is designed to produce a stronger immune response or may offer better protection than standard-dose vaccines. These include high-dose, recombinant, adjuvanted, and mRNA vaccine options. New mRNA flu vaccine: mFlusiva is the first mRNA flu vaccine, approved for adults 50 and older. Clinical trials found it was more effective than a standard-dose flu vaccine, although that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s better than other vaccines recommended for older adults. RSV Who should get an immunization? All adults 75 and older. Adults ages 50 to 74 who are at increased risk of severe RSV because of underlying health conditions or other risk factors. People who are 32 to 36 weeks pregnant during RSV season, generally September through January in most of the U.S., to help protect their babies after birth. Infants younger than 8 months entering their first RSV season whose birthing parent was not vaccinated during pregnancy, whose birthing parent’s vaccination status is unknown, or who were born less than 14 days after maternal vaccination. Some children ages 8 to 19 months who are at increased risk of severe RSV and entering their second RSV season. What RSV immunizations are available? Eligible adults can receive an RSV vaccine. Unlike COVID-19 and flu vaccines, RSV vaccines aren’t recommended every year. People who have already received an RSV vaccine generally don’t need another dose. Infants get an antibody medication — not a vaccine — that helps protect against severe RSV. Most infants don’t need both maternal vaccination and an antibody product. more on this topic Guest opinion: As vaccine guidance shifts, Wisconsin families should follow the evidence Wisconsin health department continues to urge new COVID-19 vaccine for anyone over 6 months old When’s the best time to get vaccinated against COVID-19 and the flu this season? Both Malani and Chin-Hong agree that earlier in the fall is an ideal time to get vaccinated against COVID-19 and the flu. It’s also safe (and convenient) to get both vaccines at the same appointment. Chin-Hong says the timing is particularly important for the flu vaccine this year because flu activity is increasing earlier than usual. “It’s important to get vaccinated before respiratory virus infections start to increase,” Malani said. “Especially since it takes a few weeks to provide a protective immune response.” Are COVID-19, flu and RSV vaccines free this year? Yes. Most major health insurance plans, including Medicaid, Medicare and CHIP, are expected to cover COVID-19, flu and RSV vaccines at no cost to eligible patients. However, coverage can vary depending on your insurance plan, age and where you get vaccinated. If you have private insurance, check that your health care provider or pharmacy is in network to avoid unexpected costs. If you’re uninsured, you may be able to get vaccinated for free or at a reduced cost through your local health department or a community health center. Children who qualify can also receive free vaccines through the federal Vaccines for Children program. Britannica Editors Last updated Nov. 4, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Top Questions What is Katalin Karikó famous for? Hungarian-born biochemist Katalin Karikó is best known for her pioneering research into RNA therapeutics, particularly the development of messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines. Karikó’s research showed how modified mRNA nucleosides could be used to direct the immune system against particular pathogens, a discovery that paved the way for the first mRNA-based vaccines, introduced in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. What major award did Katalin Karikó receive in 2023? Hungarian-born biochemist Katalin Karikó was awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for her discoveries relating to mRNA nucleosides. She shared the prize with her colleague American immunologist Drew Weissman. What degree does Katalin Karikó have? Katalin Karikó earned a bachelor’s degree in biology in 1978 and completed a Ph.D. in biochemistry four years later. It was during this period that she first encountered the newly identified molecule known as mRNA, which carries instructions that direct cellular activity.. What was the company Karikó and Weissman founded to commercialize non-immunogenic, nucleoside-modified RNA technology? In 2006, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman started a company called RNARx, which aimed to commercialize non-immunogenic, nucleoside-modified RNA. The researchers eventually licensed the technology to two biotechnology companies, Moderna and BioNTech. In 2013 Karikó took a position as senior vice president at BioNTech, overseeing the company’s work on mRNA. Katalin Karikó (born January 17, 1955, Kisújszállás, Hungary) is a Hungarian-born biochemist known for her pioneering research into RNA (ribonucleic acid) therapeutics, particularly the development of messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines. Karikó’s investigation into the ability of mRNA nucleosides (structural subunits of nucleic acids) to trigger immune responses against specific pathogens (disease-causing agents) greatly facilitated the development of the first mRNA vaccines—a breakthrough that occurred in 2021, during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. For their discoveries relating to mRNA nucleosides, which opened the way to the development of effective COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, Karikó and her colleague American immunologist Drew Weissman were awarded the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Education and early career Quick Facts Born: January 17, 1955 Affiliation: University of Szeged, Hungary; Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania Notable achievements: Contributed to discoveries relating to messenger RNA (mRNA) nucleosides and the development of mRNA vaccines. Major awards: 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine Karikó grew up in a small village in Hungary, where from an early age she expressed an interest in nature and excelled academically in science. She earned a bachelor’s degree in science in 1978 and a Ph.D. in biochemistry from the University of Szeged. Karikó then accepted a position at the Biological Research Centre (BRC), Szeged. There she studied the antiviral activity of short segments of RNA and began her investigations of modified nucleosides, a type of synthetic mRNA in which specific nucleosides have been altered or replaced, typically with either synthetic nucleosides or naturally modified nucleosides. In 1985, with no further funding to support her research at the BRC, Karikó moved to the United States, where she accepted a position as a postdoctoral researcher at Temple University in Philadelphia. Four years later she took a position at the University of Pennsylvania (Penn). There, with American cardiologist Elliot Barnathan, she demonstrated that mRNA, when inserted into cells, could be used to direct the production of new proteins. The breakthrough inspired her to pursue the study of mRNA-based gene therapy. Discover the fascinating events that shaped the world, straight from our editors. SIGN UP Thank you for signing up! By clicking “Sign Up”, you consent to the Britannica Privacy Policy and Terms of Use. mRNA research By the late 1990s, however, Karikó’s work on mRNA and gene therapy had stalled—again, for lack of funding. She considered leaving Penn for another research institution or pursuing different work entirely, but then she began collaborating at Penn with Weissman. Both researchers were interested in the possibility of using mRNA to stimulate the body to develop immunity against viral pathogens. In initial studies, they discovered that mRNA is highly immunogenic, provoking counterproductive immune responses in the body. However, when Karikó carried out experiments with a different type of RNA molecule, transfer RNA (tRNA), she did not observe the same immunogenic effects. That observation encouraged her and Weissman to experiment with modified nucleosides, which she had known about from her work at the BRC. The researchers went on to identify associations between specific modified mRNA nucleosides and reduced immunogenicity—a breakthrough that resulted in a technology known as non-immunogenic, nucleoside-modified RNA, which was developed and patented (2005) by Karikó and Weissman. Karikó and Weissman subsequently started a company called RNARx, which aimed to commercialize non-immunogenic, nucleoside-modified RNA. The researchers eventually licensed the technology to two biotechnology companies, Moderna and BioNTech. In 2013 Karikó took a position as senior vice president at BioNTech, overseeing the company’s work on mRNA. In the following years, although both companies had multiple RNA therapeutics in clinical trials, none had yet proved successful. In 2021, however, a major breakthrough came during the COVID-19 pandemic, fueled by the urgency to develop a vaccine that could help prevent or reduce the severity of infection with SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. Unlike traditional vaccine development, the generation of mRNA vaccines is relatively rapid, relying primarily on synthetic technologies, without any need for actual virus particles. Within months of obtaining the genetic code of SARS-CoV-2, scientists at Moderna and Pfizer-BioNTech had experimental mRNA vaccines ready for testing. Awards In addition to the Nobel Prize, Karikó’s work on RNA therapeutics was recognized with numerous honours, including the Lewis S. Rosenstiel Award for Distinguished Work in Basic Medical Research (2020), the Lasker-DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award (2021), and the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize (2021); all three awards were shared with Weissman. Log in Springer Medicine Top BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth Neonatal SARS-CoV-2 positivity and short-term outcomes Open Access 11-08-2026 Research Published in: Authors Letícia Veríssimo Dutra Giovana Leite Gonçalves Mariliza Henrique Silva Cibele Wolf Lebrão Fernando Luiz Affonso‐Fonseca Fabíola Isabel Suano‐Souza Published in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth | Issue 1/2026 Login to get access Abstract Background Neonatal SARS-CoV-2 positivity among newborns born to infected mothers appears to be uncommon, and factors associated with neonatal positivity and short-term outcomes remain incompletely understood. Objective This study aimed to compare short-term outcomes between SARS-CoV-2-positive and SARS-CoV-2-negative newborns born to mothers with COVID-19 during pregnancy. Methods In this matched case–control study, 263 pregnant women with COVID-19 were identified during the study period, and 218 newborns underwent RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 within the first 48 h of life. Among them, 23 newborns tested positive and were matched (1:2) with 46 newborns who tested negative according to clinically relevant maternal and neonatal characteristics, including the interval between maternal infection and delivery, maternal disease severity, gestational age, newborn sex, and birth weight appropriateness for gestational age. Results The mean gestational age and birth weight of the newborns were 38.2 ± 1.7 weeks and 2994.2 ± 464.5 g, respectively. Fifteen newborns (21.7%) experienced complications during hospitalization, most commonly hypotonia/hypoactivity (13.0%) and early respiratory distress (10.1%). Respiratory distress was associated with neonatal SARS-CoV-2 positivity (OR = 21.31; 95% CI 2.24–201.68; p = 0.008). In addition, maternal COVID-19 infection occurring closer to delivery was associated with an increased likelihood of neonatal SARS-CoV-2 positivity (OR = 1.007; 95% CI 1.001–1.014; p = 0.026). Conclusions SARS-CoV-2-positive newborns appeared to experience respiratory complications more frequently during hospitalization, while maternal infection closer to delivery was associated with neonatal positivity. Given the observational design and relatively small sample size, these findings should be interpreted with caution. records.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, November 8, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology Virtual Screen Spotlights Antiviral Drugs and Plant Compounds Against SARS-CoV-2 Proteins by November 6, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Virtual Screen Spotlights Antiviral Drugs and Plant Compounds Against SARS-CoV-2 Proteins Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have used molecular docking software to screen 128 compounds, including 89 FDA-approved antiviral drugs and 39 plant-derived molecules, against three SARS-CoV-2 proteins: the nsp15 endoribonuclease, the main protease, and the nsp16-nsp10 complex. The computational study, published in the journal Green Technology, Resilience, and Sustainability, was designed as a proactive exercise in drug repurposing, aiming to build a pre-screened pool of candidates that could be rapidly evaluated if a similar viral outbreak were to recur. The work is entirely in silico, meaning the results reflect predicted binding interactions rather than measured antiviral activity in cells, animals, or patients. The team, led by Triveni Singirisetty and colleagues, docked the compound libraries onto crystal structures obtained from the Protein Data Bank: 6VWW for nsp15, 6Y84 for the main protease, and 6W4H for the nsp16-nsp10 complex. Docking was performed with the licensed Schrödinger 2021_2 Glide Maestro tool, and the results were ranked by glide scores and expressed in binding energy values of kilocalories per mole. Before docking, the selected proteins were validated with Ramachandran plots, which assess whether the torsional angles of amino acid residues fall within favored or disfavored regions, and the binding sites were identified either through Glide’s sitemap tool or, for the nsp16-nsp10 complex, by anchoring the grid to the co-crystallized ligand S-adenosylmethionine, known as SAM. Each target plays a distinct role in the viral life cycle. Nsp15 is a nidoviral uridylate-specific endoribonuclease whose hexamerized form binds RNA to execute its cleavage activity, and it requires metal ions such as manganese or magnesium as cofactors. The main protease is central to processing viral polyproteins, and the nsp16-nsp10 complex carries out 2′-O-methyltransferase activity, with nsp10 activating the methyltransferase function of nsp16. Because two-thirds of the coronavirus genome encodes non-structural proteins that drive replication, the authors argue that simultaneously targeting these three proteins offers a strategy to interfere with RNA processing, protein maturation, and RNA capping at different stages of the viral cycle. Against nsp15, the top-ranked antiviral drugs by glide score were remdesivir at -7.228, ribavirin at -6.988, letermovir at -6.96, favipiravir at -6.823, and idoxuridine at -6.788. Remdesivir formed hydrogen bond interactions with the residues TYR 89, GLY 165, and SER 198, along with a hydrophobic interaction with LYS 90. When binding energy was considered instead, zidovudine stood out with a value of -72.11 kcal/mol, and compounds such as cobicistat, ritonavir, saquinavir, telaprevir, and daclatasvir also showed energies in the -60 kcal/mol range, leading the authors to suggest these deserve further in vitro study. The plant-derived library produced notable results at the same target. Epigallocatechin achieved a glide score of -7.596, amentoflavone -7.417, and quercetin -7.408, all stronger than remdesivir’s -7.22 at nsp15. Ent-epiafzelechin followed at -6.944. The authors observed that amentoflavone and ent-epiafzelechin interact with distinct sets of amino acid residues, including GLU 203, ASP 268, THR 167, TYR 279, ASP 297, and VAL 295, and they speculate that such interaction patterns might interfere with the hexamerization that nsp15 requires for full endoribonuclease activity. Two natural compounds, saikosaponin A and vitamin B2, did not fit into the nsp15 active site and were excluded from that ranking. Docking against the main protease yielded a different hierarchy. Adefovir led the antiviral drugs with a glide score of -7.527, followed by entecavir at -7.141, penciclovir at -7.07, ganciclovir at -6.852, and tenofovir at -6.624. Adefovir formed hydrogen bonds with MET 6, ASP 153, TYR 154, and ARG 298, plus hydrophobic contact with PHE 8. The study noted that glide energies at this target were generally lower than those observed for nsp15, though four drugs, cobicistat, telaprevir, remdesivir, and raltegravir, exceeded -50 kcal/mol in binding energy. Among natural compounds, ent-epiafzelechin scored -7.03, hippomannin A -6.71, epigallocatechin -6.425, quercetin -6.141, and proanthocyanidin -6.624. Six antiviral drugs and six natural compounds, including chebulagic acid and saikosaponin A, failed to dock into the main protease active site. The nsp16-nsp10 complex was screened at the SAM binding site, using the co-crystallized SAM as a reference standard. SAM itself recorded the highest docking score of -10.06 with a glide energy of -76.49 kcal/mol. Vidarabine emerged as the closest antiviral lead at -9.399, followed by tenofovir at -8.654, telbivudine at -7.839, fosamprenavir at -7.808, and ribavirin at -7.654. Zidovudine, however, displayed the lowest binding energy of the screen at -80.07 kcal/mol, below even SAM’s -76.49, and formed an ionic bond with ASP 6897. The authors interpret this as indicating a more stable predicted zidovudine-protein complex than the SAM-protein complex, and they also flagged ritonavir, cobicistat, saquinavir, and emricasan as having comparable energies. Among natural molecules, apigenin scored -7.58, quercetin -7.316, silymarin -7.252, amentoflavone -7.182, and ent-epiafzelechin -7.142, with several sharing common residue interactions with SAM, including ASP 6912, CYS 6913, and ASP 6928. The authors place their findings in the context of a broader repurposing literature. They cite reports that remdesivir showed an EC90 of 1.76 micromolar against the virus in Vero E6 cells and that it acts on the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase by delaying chain termination. They also reference in vitro work showing that epigallocatechin gallate, a major green tea component, blocks the interaction between the viral spike protein and the ACE2 receptor, and computational studies in which flavonoids such as hesperidin and rutin showed strong affinity for viral proteins. The paper notes that repurposing can shorten development timelines, citing figures that 30 percent of repurposed drugs reach Phase II trials, that timelines shrink from 10 to 15 years to 3 to 6 years, and that costs fall by 40 to 60 percent, though these are literature-derived estimates rather than findings of the present study. The limitations of the approach are significant and acknowledged by the authors themselves. Docking scores are computational predictions of binding affinity, not proof of antiviral effect, and the paper explicitly states that the identified compounds warrant further investigation through in vitro and in vivo validation studies before any therapeutic conclusions can be drawn. The study also did not perform molecular dynamics simulations or free energy calculations, which the authors recommend as future refinements to improve binding predictions. The compound library was assembled from earlier reports rather than an exhaustive chemical space survey, and a handful of molecules failed to dock at certain targets, illustrating how ligand preparation and active site geometry can shape outcomes. As a preparedness exercise, the study offers a ranked shortlist rather than a treatment recommendation. Its practical value lies in narrowing hundreds of possibilities to a manageable set of leads, remdesivir, ribavirin, and letermovir at nsp15; adefovir, entecavir, and penciclovir at the main protease; vidarabine, tenofovir, fosamprenavir, zidovudine, and saquinavir at the SAM site; and plant molecules such as apigenin, quercetin, silymarin, amentoflavone, hippomannin A, epigallocatechin, ent-epiafzelechin, and chebulagic acid, that laboratories could prioritize for experimental testing. The authors argue that maintaining such pre-validated leads, particularly among drugs with established safety profiles, could accelerate the response to future coronavirus outbreaks, provided the computational predictions survive the rigors of laboratory and clinical validation. B., Bodapati, A., Kallam, S. D. M., Thangaswamy, S., Nelson, V. K., & Suryadevara, P. R. (2025). Drug repurposing in silico screening of antiviral drugs and evidence-based plant-derived anti-oxidant molecules targeting nsp15, main protease, and nsp16-nsp10 complex of SARS-CoV-2: strategic insights for managing future recurrence.
